paragraphs: SECTION 5.3.

Such fatherly concern runs through Dr. Gregory’s Legacy to his daughters that I undertake the task of criticism with affectionate respect. But since this little volume has many attractions to recommend it to the notice of the most respectable part of my sex, I cannot pass over in silence arguments that so plausibly support opinions which, I think, have had the most harmful effect on the morals and conduct of the female world.

His easy, familiar style particularly suits the tenor of his advice, and the melancholy tenderness that his respect for the memory of a beloved wife spreads through the whole work makes it very affecting. Yet in many passages there is a noticeable degree of concise elegance that disturbs this sympathy; we stumble upon the author when we expected to meet only the — father.

Besides, having two aims in view, he seldom kept steadily to either. Wishing to make his daughters amiable, and afraid that unhappiness would be the only result of instilling sentiments that might draw them out of the track of ordinary life without enabling them to act with a matching independence and dignity, he checks the natural flow of his thoughts and advises neither one thing nor the other.
In the preface he tells them a sad truth, “that they will hear, at least once in their lives, the genuine sentiments of a man, who has no interest in deceiving them.”

Unhappy woman! What can be expected of you, when the beings on whom you are said by nature to depend for reason and support all have an interest in deceiving you! This is the root of the evil that has spread a corroding mildew over all your virtues and, blighting your opening faculties in the bud, has made you the weak thing you are! It is this separate interest — this insidious state of warfare — that undermines morality and divides mankind!

If love has made some women wretched — how many more has the cold, meaningless traffic of gallantry made vain and useless! Yet this heartless attention to the sex is thought so manly, so polite, that until society is organized very differently, I fear, this relic of gothic manners will not give way to a more reasonable and affectionate mode of conduct. Moreover, to strip it of its imaginary dignity, I must point out that in the most civilized states of Europe this lip-service is extremely widespread, and goes together with an extreme looseness of morals. In Portugal, the country I particularly have in mind, it takes precedence over the most serious moral obligations; for a man is seldom assassinated while he is in the company of a woman. The savage hand of violence is unnerved by this chivalrous spirit; and if the stroke of vengeance cannot be held back — the lady is begged to pardon the rudeness and to go in peace, though she may be spattered with her husband’s or her brother’s blood.
I shall pass over his remarks on religion, because I intend to discuss that subject in a separate chapter.

His remarks on behaviour, though many of them are very sensible, I entirely disapprove of, because they seem to me to begin, as it were, at the wrong end. A cultivated understanding and an affectionate heart will never need starched rules of decorum; something more substantial than mere seemliness will be the result; and without understanding, the behaviour recommended here would be sheer affectation. Decorum, indeed, is the one thing needful! Decorum is to take the place of nature and banish all simplicity and variety of character from the female world. Yet what good can all this superficial advice achieve? It is, however, much easier to prescribe this or that way of behaving than to set the reason to work; but once the mind has been stocked with useful knowledge, and strengthened by being used, the regulation of behaviour may safely be left to its guidance.

Why, for instance, should the following caution be given, when artifice of every kind must contaminate the mind? And why entangle the great motives of action, which reason and religion join equally in enforcing, with pitiful worldly dodges and sleight-of-hand tricks to win the applause of gaping, tasteless fools? “Be even cautious in displaying your good sense.* It will be thought you assume a superiority over the rest of the company — But if you happen to have any learning keep it a profound secret, especially from the men, who generally look with a jealous and malignant eye on a woman of great parts, and a cultivated understanding.” If men of real merit, as he goes on to observe, are above such baseness, why must the behaviour of the whole sex be tuned to please fools, or men who, having little claim to respect as individuals, choose to keep close ranks in their phalanx? Men, indeed, who insist on their common superiority when they have only this superiority of sex are certainly very excusable.
(*Footnote. Let women once acquire good sense — and if it deserves the name, it will teach them how to use it; otherwise, what use will it be?)
There would be no end to rules of behaviour if it were right always to adopt the tone of the company; for, with the key forever changing, a FLAT would often pass for a NATURAL note.

Surely it would have been wiser to advise women to improve themselves until they rose above the fumes of vanity, and then to let public opinion come round — for where are rules of accommodation to stop? The narrow path of truth and virtue turns neither to the right nor to the left; it is a straightforward matter, and those who are earnestly pursuing their road may leap over many decorous prejudices without leaving modesty behind. Make the heart clean and give the head employment, and I will venture to predict that there will be nothing offensive in the behaviour.

The fashionable air that so many young people are eager to acquire always strikes me as being like the studied poses in some modern prints, copied with tasteless servility from antique statues: the soul is left out, and none of the parts are bound together by what may properly be called character. This varnish of fashion, which seldom adheres very closely to good sense, may dazzle the weak; but nature left to itself will seldom disgust the wise. Besides, when a woman has sense enough not to pretend to anything she does not understand to some degree, there is no need for her to resolve to hide her talents under a bushel. Let things take their natural course, and all will be well.

It is this system of dissimulation, running through the whole volume, that I despise. Women are always to SEEM to be this and that — yet virtue might address them in the words of Hamlet: “Seems! I know not seems! — Have that within that passeth show!”

The same tone recurs, for in another place, after recommending delicacy (without drawing sufficient distinctions), he adds, “The men will complain of your reserve. They will assure you that a franker behaviour would make you more amiable. But, trust me, they are not sincere when they tell you so. I acknowledge that on some occasions it might render you more agreeable as companions, but it would make you less amiable as women: an important distinction, which many of your sex are not aware of.”

This desire always to be women is the very consciousness that degrades the sex. Except with a lover, I must emphatically repeat an earlier observation — it would be well if they were simply agreeable or rational companions. But in this respect his advice is even inconsistent with a passage which I intend to quote with the most marked approval.

“The sentiment, that a woman may allow all innocent freedoms, provided her virtue is secure, is both grossly indelicate and dangerous, and has proved fatal to many of your sex.” I entirely agree with this opinion. A man or a woman of any feeling must always wish to convince a beloved person that it is the caresses of the individual, not of the sex, that are received and returned with pleasure, and that it is the heart, rather than the senses, that is moved. Without this natural delicacy, love becomes a selfish personal gratification that soon degrades the character.

I carry this sentiment further still. Affection, when love is out of the question, justifies many personal endearments which, flowing naturally from an innocent heart, give life to behaviour; but physical familiarity prompted by appetite, gallantry or vanity is despicable. When a man squeezes the hand of a pretty woman he has never seen before as he hands her into a carriage, she will regard such an impertinent liberty as an insult, if she has any true delicacy, instead of being flattered by this meaningless homage to beauty. These are the privileges of friendship, or of the momentary homage the heart pays to virtue when it suddenly flashes into view — mere high spirits have no claim to the kindnesses of affection.

Wishing to feed the affections with what now feeds vanity, I would gladly persuade my sex to act from simpler principles. Let them deserve love, and they will obtain it, though they may never be told that “The power of a fine woman over the hearts of men, of men of the finest parts, is even beyond what she conceives.”

I have already noted the narrow cautions about duplicity, female softness and delicacy of constitution; for these are the changes he rings round and round without ceasing — in a more decorous manner than Rousseau, it is true, but it all comes back to the same point, and anyone who takes the trouble to analyze these sentiments will find the first principles not quite so delicate as the superstructure.
The subject of amusements is treated too briefly, but in the same spirit.

When I come to treat friendship, love and marriage, it will be seen that we differ materially in opinion. I shall not, then, anticipate what I have to say on these important subjects, but will confine my remarks to their general tenor: to that cautious family prudence, to those narrow views of partial, unenlightened affection, which shut out pleasure and improvement by vainly trying to ward off sorrow and error — and which, by guarding the heart and mind in this way, destroy all their energy as well. It is far better to be often deceived than never to trust; to be disappointed in love than never to love; to lose a husband’s fondness than to forfeit his esteem.

It would be a happy thing for the world, and of course for individuals, if all this fruitless anxiety to attain worldly happiness on a narrow plan were turned into an eager desire to improve the understanding. “Wisdom is the principal thing: THEREFORE get wisdom; and with all thy gettings get understanding.” “How long ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity, and hate knowledge?” So Wisdom says to the daughters of men!
